inputs.system:
You are BIE's book-understanding section: an expert teacher of Science and Technology for UPSC / State PCS aspirants preparing for UPSC / State PCS.
You read one page of a book chapter with two eyes, the page's native text blocks and the page image, and turn it into a complete,
question-based teacher's understanding. Later BIE sections build the video lessons, the chapter game and the notes only from what you
capture, so anything you miss is missing from the whole course.

Course: "10. Tissues and Its Types" · subject: Science and Technology · learners: UPSC / State PCS aspirants · exam: UPSC / State PCS · learner language: Hinglish.
Your output is internal to BIE: write it in clear English and keep the book's own terms and spellings.

Navin's rules for this section (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never shorten work to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, completeness wins.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. Keep outside explanations at standard textbook level for these learners and avoid absolute words (always, only, never, all, every) unless the book uses them.
[S1-08] Give every item its true content type (definition, fact, process, structure, comparison, classification, timeline, cause_effect, formula, data, example, question). The content type decides later how the video shows it, how the game makes it playable and how the notes draw it, so choose by what the content is, not by how it is printed.
[S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.
[S1-11] Where the text layer and the image disagree (garbled symbols, missing words, wrong order), report the disagreement. Trust the image for symbols, layout and diagrams, and the text layer for spelling when it is clean.

How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part) with a reason each, and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "".
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the list given.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree).
  - content_type: what the content really is (definition, fact, process, structure, comparison, classification, timeline, cause_effect,
    formula, data, example, question, other).
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (see S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside". BIE's code checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how"; a process needs "how"; a comparison or classification needs "compare" or
    "difference".
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.
- text_image_disagreements: where the text layer and the image differ.
Reply with the JSON object only.

output.page_summary: The page compares the three types of muscular tissue in a table. Skeletal muscle is in the skeleton, gives movement, heat and posture, is striated, multinucleated with eccentric nuclei and parallel fibres, and is voluntary. Cardiac muscle is in the heart, pumps blood continuously, is striated with one central nucleus, and is involuntary. Visceral (smooth) muscle is in the G.I. tract, uterus, eye and blood vessels, drives peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size and hair erection, has no striations and one central nucleus, and is involuntary. Below are NCERT Fig. 6.10 on types of connective tissue (blood cells, compact bone, hyaline cartilage, areolar tissue, adipose tissue) and a diagram of how neurons transmit impulses: dendrites, cell body and nucleus, axon carrying an electrical signal, axon tips and the synapse with the next neuron's dendrites.

items.content: Three Types of Muscular Tissue
items.exam_note: Heading only.

items.content: Table comparing the three muscular tissues (Skeletal, Cardiac, Visceral/smooth muscle), each with a small cell illustration. The columns are Location, Function, Appearance and Control.

teacher_understanding.question: What does this table compare?
teacher_understanding.answer: It compares skeletal, cardiac and visceral (smooth) muscle on four features: where each is found, what it does, how it looks under a microscope (striations, nuclei) and whether it is under voluntary control.

teacher_understanding.question: Which feature separates skeletal muscle from the other two?
teacher_understanding.answer: Control. Only skeletal muscle is voluntary, while cardiac and smooth muscle are involuntary. Skeletal muscle is also the only multinucleated one; the other two have one central nucleus.

teacher_understanding.question: What do cardiac and skeletal muscle share, and what do cardiac and smooth muscle share?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac and skeletal muscle are both striated. Cardiac and smooth muscle are both involuntary and have one central nucleus. Cardiac muscle is therefore the bridge: it looks like skeletal muscle but is controlled like smooth muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: Why do striations appear in some muscles?
teacher_understanding.answer: Striations are alternating light and dark bands. They come from the regular, repeating arrangement of the contractile proteins actin and myosin. Smooth muscle has these proteins but not in a regular banded order, so it looks unstriped.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does it make sense that heart and gut muscles are involuntary?
teacher_understanding.answer: Heartbeat and digestion must continue without conscious thought, even during sleep. They are controlled by the autonomic nervous system and by the muscle's own rhythm rather than by our will.

prerequisites: difference between voluntary and involuntary actions
items.exam_note: This is a classic UPSC/PCS comparison. Expect odd-one-out and matching questions on striations, nuclei, control and location (e.g. 'which muscle is striated but involuntary').

items.content: Skeletal | Location: skeleton | Function: movement, heat, posture | Appearance: striated, multi-nucleated (eccentric), fibers parallel | Control: voluntary

teacher_understanding.question: Where is skeletal muscle found?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is attached to the skeleton (bones), usually through tendons.

teacher_understanding.question: What are its functions?
teacher_understanding.answer: It produces movement, generates body heat and maintains posture.

teacher_understanding.question: How does skeletal muscle produce heat?
teacher_understanding.answer: Contraction uses ATP, and part of that energy is released as heat. This is why shivering, which is rapid involuntary skeletal muscle contraction, warms the body.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a skeletal fibre multinucleated?
teacher_understanding.answer: Each skeletal fibre forms by the fusion of many embryonic cells, so it is long and keeps many nuclei. The nuclei lie at the edge (eccentric/peripheral) under the cell membrane.

teacher_understanding.question: Which type of control does it have?
teacher_understanding.answer: Voluntary: it contracts when we consciously decide to move, under the somatic nervous system. It is also called striated or voluntary muscle.

items.exam_note: The striated + multinucleate + voluntary combination is a frequently tested identification.

items.content: Cardiac | Location: heart | Function: pump blood continuously | Appearance: striated, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary

teacher_understanding.question: Where is cardiac muscle found?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is found only in the heart wall.

teacher_understanding.question: What does it do?
teacher_understanding.answer: It pumps blood continuously, throughout life, without rest.

teacher_understanding.question: How can it work continuously without tiring?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac cells have many mitochondria and a rich blood supply for steady aerobic energy. They are also branched and joined by intercalated discs, so they contract together in a rhythm that includes a brief rest between beats.

teacher_understanding.question: What makes cardiac muscle a special case?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is striated like skeletal muscle, yet involuntary like smooth muscle, and its cells have one central nucleus.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is it involuntary?
teacher_understanding.answer: The heartbeat starts in the heart's own pacemaker (the SA node). The autonomic nerves only speed it up or slow it down, so we cannot stop the heart at will.

items.exam_note: 'Striated but involuntary' is a favourite odd-one-out fact.

items.content: Visceral (smooth muscle) | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: Peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary

teacher_understanding.question: Where is smooth muscle found?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is found in the walls of hollow internal organs, the viscera (hence the name 'visceral'). Examples are the G.I. tract, uterus, eye (iris) and blood vessels.

teacher_understanding.question: How does each function link to its location?
teacher_understanding.answer: In the gut it produces peristalsis, the wave-like push of food. In blood vessels it narrows or widens them, which controls blood pressure. In the iris it changes pupil size. In the skin, the small muscles attached to hairs make hairs stand on end (goosebumps).

teacher_understanding.question: How does peristalsis move food?
teacher_understanding.answer: Rings of smooth muscle contract behind the food and relax ahead of it. This creates a wave that pushes the food forward slowly.

teacher_understanding.question: What does smooth muscle look like?
teacher_understanding.answer: It has no striations, and its cells are spindle-shaped with one central nucleus (see the spindle cell drawn in the table).

teacher_understanding.question: Why is it called unstriated or involuntary muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: It has no bands, and it works without our will under autonomic control.

prerequisites: iris and pupil of the eye
items.exam_note: The location and function list (peristalsis, pupil, blood pressure, hair erection) is often asked in matching questions.

items.content: NCERT Fig. 6.10, a composite of five panels. (a) Types of blood cells: different white blood corpuscles (Neutrophil, Eosinophil, Basophil, Lymphocyte, Monocyte), Platelets and a Red blood corpuscle. (b) Compact bone, with concentric rings around a Haversian canal and canaliculi. (c) Hyaline cartilage, with chondrocytes in hyaline matrix. (d) Areolar tissue, with reticular fibre, fibroblast, macrophage, collagen fibre, mast cell and plasma cell. (e) Adipose tissue, with adipocytes holding fat droplets and nuclei pushed aside.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the figure show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows five types of connective tissue: blood, compact bone, hyaline cartilage, areolar tissue and adipose tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: What common plan do all these tissues share?
teacher_understanding.answer: In each, cells are scattered within an intercellular matrix. Blood has a fluid matrix (plasma). Bone has a hard matrix with calcium and phosphorus. Cartilage has a firm, flexible matrix. Areolar tissue has fibres in a jelly-like matrix. Adipose tissue is mostly fat-filled cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are such different tissues grouped as 'connective'?
teacher_understanding.answer: They all arise from embryonic mesoderm, and all connect, support, bind or transport between other tissues. The nature of the matrix decides each tissue's role.

items.exam_note: Examples of connective tissue and their cell types (osteocyte, chondrocyte, adipocyte) are often asked.

items.content: Different white blood corpuscles: Neutrophil (polymorphonuclear leucocyte), Eosinophil, Basophil; labels Cytoplasm and Nucleus point to parts of a WBC

teacher_understanding.question: What are neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are granular white blood cells (granulocytes) with lobed nuclei. The neutrophil is called polymorphonuclear because its nucleus has many lobes.

teacher_understanding.question: How does each help the body?
teacher_understanding.answer: Neutrophils engulf bacteria (phagocytosis). Eosinophils fight parasites and are involved in allergy. Basophils release histamine during inflammation.

items.exam_note: The most abundant WBC (neutrophil) is a common question.

items.content: Lymphocyte, Monocyte, Platelets

teacher_understanding.question: What are lymphocytes and monocytes?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are agranular WBCs. Lymphocytes (B and T cells) give specific immunity, including antibody production. Monocytes become macrophages that engulf microbes.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are platelets important?
teacher_understanding.answer: Platelets are cell fragments that help blood clot at a wound and stop bleeding.

items.exam_note: Platelets and clotting; lymphocytes and antibodies.

items.content: Red blood corpuscle, pointing to a round biconcave cell without a nucleus

teacher_understanding.question: What does the RBC do?
teacher_understanding.answer: It carries oxygen using haemoglobin.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does a mammalian RBC lack a nucleus?
teacher_understanding.answer: Losing the nucleus leaves more space for haemoglobin, and the biconcave shape increases surface area for gas exchange.

items.exam_note: An enucleated RBC is a frequent fact.

items.content: Haversian canal (contains blood vessels and nerve fibres), pointing to the central canal of the concentric rings of bone

teacher_understanding.question: What is the Haversian canal?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a central channel in compact bone that carries blood vessels and nerve fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does bone need such canals?
teacher_understanding.answer: Bone is hard and living. Its cells need nutrients and oxygen, and the canals bring blood deep into the hard matrix.

items.exam_note: The Haversian system is characteristic of mammalian compact bone.

items.content: Canaliculus (contains slender process of bone cell or osteocyte)

teacher_understanding.question: What is a canaliculus?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a tiny channel in bone that holds the thin extensions of osteocytes (bone cells).

teacher_understanding.question: How do canaliculi keep bone cells alive?
teacher_understanding.answer: They connect the osteocytes to one another and to the Haversian canal, so nutrients and wastes can pass through the hard matrix.

items.exam_note: Remember: osteocyte = bone cell.

items.content: Chondrocyte and Hyaline matrix, pointing to cartilage cells and the clear surrounding matrix

teacher_understanding.question: What is hyaline cartilage made of?
teacher_understanding.answer: It consists of chondrocytes (cartilage cells) in a clear, firm matrix of proteins and sugars.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is it found?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is found at the ends of bones in joints, in the nose, the ear (as cartilage), the trachea and the larynx.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is cartilage used there instead of bone?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its matrix is firm yet flexible, so it smooths joint surfaces and gives shape that can bend.

items.exam_note: Chondrocyte = cartilage cell.

items.content: Reticular fibre, Fibroblast, Macrophage, Collagen fibre, Mast cell, Plasma cell

teacher_understanding.question: What cells and fibres make up areolar tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Fibroblasts produce the fibres (collagen and reticular). Macrophages engulf microbes. Mast cells release histamine. Plasma cells make antibodies.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is areolar tissue found?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lies between skin and muscles, around blood vessels and nerves, and in bone marrow. It fills spaces inside organs.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does it contain immune cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lies just under the skin and around organs, where microbes may enter, so it also helps repair tissues and defend the body.

items.exam_note: Areolar tissue is the 'packing' tissue between skin and muscle.

items.content: Fat droplet, Nucleus, Adipocyte, pointing to large fat-filled cells with the nucleus pushed to one side

teacher_understanding.question: What is adipose tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is connective tissue made of adipocytes, which are cells filled with fat droplets.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does it matter to the body?
teacher_understanding.answer: It stores energy as fat and acts as a thermal insulator, for example under the skin. It also cushions organs.

items.exam_note: Adipose tissue gives insulation, for example blubber in whales.

items.content: Fig. 6.10: Types of connective tissues: (a) types of blood cells, (b) compact bone, (c) hyaline cartilage, (d) areolar tissue, (e) adipose tissue

teacher_understanding.question: Which connective tissues does the caption list?
teacher_understanding.answer: Blood, compact bone, hyaline cartilage, areolar tissue and adipose tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How do they differ in matrix?
teacher_understanding.answer: The matrix is fluid in blood, hard in bone, firm and flexible in cartilage, loose and fibrous in areolar tissue, and mostly fat-filled cells in adipose tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is blood a connective tissue though it is fluid?
teacher_understanding.answer: It has cells in an intercellular matrix (plasma), and it connects body parts by transporting gases, nutrients and hormones.

items.exam_note: 'Blood is a connective tissue' is an exam staple.

items.content: Title: 'How do neurons transmit impulses (send message to other cells)?' Two orange neurons are shown. At the lower left, the axon of a previous neuron meets the first neuron's dendrites at a synapse (circled). The first neuron's cell body and nucleus give rise to a long axon. A blue arrow labelled 'electrical signal' runs along the axon towards its branched axon tips. The tips form a synapse (circled) with the dendrites of the next neuron, whose cell body and nucleus are labelled. The sequence is dendrites → cell body → axon → axon tips → synapse → next neuron's dendrites.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the diagram show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows the path of a nerve impulse through one neuron and across a synapse to the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the impulse travel?
teacher_understanding.answer: Dendrites receive a signal and pass it to the cell body. From there it travels along the axon as an electrical signal to the axon tips. At the synapse it is passed to the dendrites of the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the signal cross the synapse?
teacher_understanding.answer: A synapse is a tiny gap. The electrical signal reaching the axon tips causes release of chemicals (neurotransmitters), which cross the gap and start a new electrical signal in the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the impulse move in one direction only?
teacher_understanding.answer: Neurotransmitters are released only from axon tips and received only by the next neuron's dendrites, so the message flows one way.

items.exam_note: The direction of impulse flow and the parts of a neuron (dendrite, axon, synapse) are frequently asked.

items.content: axon of previous neuron, pointing to the incoming fibre at the left that ends at the first synapse

teacher_understanding.question: What is the 'axon of previous neuron'?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the axon of the neuron that sends the message into the first neuron shown.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is it shown?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows that neurons form chains, with one neuron's output becoming the next neuron's input.

items.exam_note: Shows that neurons connect in chains.

items.where_on_page: neuron diagram, circled at lower left and upper middle
items.content: synapse, pointing to the circled junctions between the axon ends and the dendrites of the next neuron

teacher_understanding.question: What is a synapse?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the junction between the axon tip of one neuron and the dendrite of the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: How is a message passed there?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is passed chemically, through neurotransmitters released into the gap.

items.exam_note: The definition of a synapse is commonly asked.

items.content: neuron cell body, pointing to the central star-shaped part of each neuron

teacher_understanding.question: What is the cell body?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the main part of the neuron (cyton). It contains the nucleus and cytoplasm.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is it essential?
teacher_understanding.answer: It keeps the neuron alive by making proteins, and it combines the incoming signals before passing them to the axon.

items.exam_note: Part of a neuron.

items.where_on_page: neuron diagram, inside each cell body
items.content: nucleus, pointing to the dark dot in each neuron cell body

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the neuron's nucleus?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is in the cell body.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does this matter?
teacher_understanding.answer: The nucleus controls the cell. Mature neurons generally do not divide, so damage is hard to repair.

items.exam_note: The nucleus lies in the cyton.

items.where_on_page: neuron diagram, bottom of first neuron
items.content: dendrites, pointing to the short branched projections around the first neuron's cell body

teacher_understanding.question: What are dendrites?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are short, branched extensions of the cell body that receive signals.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are they highly branched?
teacher_understanding.answer: Branching gives more surface area to receive signals from many neurons.

items.exam_note: Dendrites receive; the axon carries the signal away.

items.content: axon, pointing to the long single fibre from the first neuron's cell body towards the next neuron

teacher_understanding.question: What is the axon?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a long single fibre that carries the impulse away from the cell body.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the signal travel fast along it?
teacher_understanding.answer: Many axons are wrapped in a myelin sheath, which speeds up conduction of the impulse.

items.exam_note: The axon is the longest part of a neuron.

items.where_on_page: neuron diagram, blue arrow along the axon
items.content: electrical signal, a blue arrow running along the axon from the cell body towards the axon tips

teacher_understanding.question: What is the electrical signal?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the nerve impulse moving along the axon.

teacher_understanding.question: How is it generated?
teacher_understanding.answer: Ions such as sodium and potassium move across the neuron membrane, and this creates a travelling change in voltage.

items.exam_note: Impulses are electrical along the axon and chemical at the synapse.

teacher_understanding.answer: They are the terminal branches of the axon that form synapses.

teacher_understanding.answer: They release neurotransmitters to pass the message on to the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.answer: They start a new impulse in the second neuron, which then repeats the same path.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is skeletal muscle found?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is attached to the skeleton (bones), usually through tendons, so its pull moves the bones at joints.

teacher_understanding.question: What are its functions?
teacher_understanding.answer: It produces movement, generates body heat and maintains posture.

teacher_understanding.question: How does skeletal muscle produce heat?
teacher_understanding.answer: Contraction uses ATP, and part of that energy is released as heat. This is why shivering, which is rapid skeletal muscle contraction, warms the body.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a skeletal fibre multinucleated?
teacher_understanding.answer: Each fibre forms by the fusion of many embryonic cells, so it is long and keeps many nuclei. The book describes these nuclei as eccentric, meaning they lie at the edge of the fibre and not in the centre.

teacher_understanding.question: How does skeletal muscle differ from cardiac and smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the only one of the three that is voluntary and the only one that is multi-nucleated. Cardiac and smooth muscle both have one central nucleus and are involuntary. It shares striations with cardiac muscle but not with smooth muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: Which type of control does it have?
teacher_understanding.answer: Voluntary control: it contracts when we consciously decide to move, through the somatic nervous system.

replace_items.exam_note: The combination 'striated + multinucleate + voluntary' is a frequently tested identification.

replace_items.content: Cardiac | Location: heart | Function: pump blood continuously | Appearance: striated, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary

teacher_understanding.question: Where is cardiac muscle found?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is found in the heart wall.

teacher_understanding.question: What does it do?
teacher_understanding.answer: It pumps blood continuously throughout life.

teacher_understanding.question: How can it work continuously without tiring?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac cells have many mitochondria and a rich blood supply, which give steady aerobic energy. They are branched and joined by intercalated discs, so they contract together in a rhythm with a brief relaxation between beats.

teacher_understanding.question: How does cardiac muscle compare with skeletal and smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: It resembles skeletal muscle in being striated. It resembles smooth muscle in being involuntary and having one central nucleus. It is therefore a mix of both, and it is the 'striated but involuntary' odd one out.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is it involuntary?
teacher_understanding.answer: The heartbeat starts in the heart's own pacemaker (the SA node). Autonomic nerves only speed it up or slow it down, so we cannot stop the heart at will.

replace_items.exam_note: 'Striated but involuntary' is a favourite odd-one-out fact.

replace_items.content: Visceral (smooth muscle) | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: Peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary

teacher_understanding.question: Where is smooth muscle found?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is found in the walls of internal organs (the viscera, hence the name 'visceral'): the G.I. tract, uterus, eye and blood vessels.

teacher_understanding.question: How does each function link to its location?
teacher_understanding.answer: In the gut it drives peristalsis. In blood vessels it narrows or widens them and so controls blood pressure. In the iris it changes pupil size. The tiny muscles attached to hairs erect the hairs, producing goosebumps.

teacher_understanding.question: How does peristalsis move food?
teacher_understanding.answer: Rings of smooth muscle contract behind the food and relax ahead of it, creating a wave that pushes the food forward.

teacher_understanding.question: How does smooth muscle differ from skeletal and cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the only one of the three with no striations. It differs from skeletal muscle in having one central nucleus and in being involuntary. It shares both of these features with cardiac muscle, but it lacks cardiac muscle's striations.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is it also called unstriated or involuntary muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows no bands, because its contractile proteins are not arranged in a regular repeating pattern. It also works without our will, under autonomic control.

output.page_summary: The page compares the three types of muscular tissue in a table. Skeletal muscle is in the skeleton, gives movement, heat and posture, is striated, multinucleated with eccentric nuclei and parallel fibres, and is voluntary. Cardiac muscle is in the heart, pumps blood continuously, is striated with one central nucleus, and is involuntary. Visceral (smooth) muscle is in the G.I. tract, uterus, eye and blood vessels, drives peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size and hair erection, has no striations and one central nucleus, and is involuntary. Below are NCERT Fig. 6.10 on types of connective tissue (blood cells, compact bone, hyaline cartilage, areolar tissue, adipose tissue) and a diagram of how neurons transmit impulses: dendrites, cell body and nucleus, axon carrying an electrical signal, axon tips and the synapse with the next neuron's dendrites.

items.content: Three Types of Muscular Tissue
items.exam_note: Heading only.

items.content: Table comparing the three muscular tissues (Skeletal, Cardiac, Visceral/smooth muscle), each with a small cell illustration. The columns are Location, Function, Appearance and Control.

teacher_understanding.question: What does this table compare?
teacher_understanding.answer: It compares skeletal, cardiac and visceral (smooth) muscle on four features: where each is found, what it does, how it looks under a microscope (striations, nuclei) and whether it is under voluntary control.

teacher_understanding.question: Which feature separates skeletal muscle from the other two?
teacher_understanding.answer: Control. Only skeletal muscle is voluntary, while cardiac and smooth muscle are involuntary. Skeletal muscle is also the only multinucleated one; the other two have one central nucleus.

teacher_understanding.question: What do cardiac and skeletal muscle share, and what do cardiac and smooth muscle share?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac and skeletal muscle are both striated. Cardiac and smooth muscle are both involuntary and have one central nucleus. Cardiac muscle is therefore the bridge: it looks like skeletal muscle but is controlled like smooth muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: Why do striations appear in some muscles?
teacher_understanding.answer: Striations are alternating light and dark bands. They come from the regular, repeating arrangement of the contractile proteins actin and myosin. Smooth muscle has these proteins but not in a regular banded order, so it looks unstriped.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does it make sense that heart and gut muscles are involuntary?
teacher_understanding.answer: Heartbeat and digestion must continue without conscious thought, even during sleep. They are controlled by the autonomic nervous system and by the muscle's own rhythm rather than by our will.

prerequisites: difference between voluntary and involuntary actions
items.exam_note: This is a classic UPSC/PCS comparison. Expect odd-one-out and matching questions on striations, nuclei, control and location (e.g. 'which muscle is striated but involuntary').

items.content: NCERT Fig. 6.10, a composite of five panels. (a) Types of blood cells: different white blood corpuscles (Neutrophil, Eosinophil, Basophil, Lymphocyte, Monocyte), Platelets and a Red blood corpuscle. (b) Compact bone, with concentric rings around a Haversian canal and canaliculi. (c) Hyaline cartilage, with chondrocytes in hyaline matrix. (d) Areolar tissue, with reticular fibre, fibroblast, macrophage, collagen fibre, mast cell and plasma cell. (e) Adipose tissue, with adipocytes holding fat droplets and nuclei pushed aside.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the figure show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows five types of connective tissue: blood, compact bone, hyaline cartilage, areolar tissue and adipose tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: What common plan do all these tissues share?
teacher_understanding.answer: In each, cells are scattered within an intercellular matrix. Blood has a fluid matrix (plasma). Bone has a hard matrix with calcium and phosphorus. Cartilage has a firm, flexible matrix. Areolar tissue has fibres in a jelly-like matrix. Adipose tissue is mostly fat-filled cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are such different tissues grouped as 'connective'?
teacher_understanding.answer: They all arise from embryonic mesoderm, and all connect, support, bind or transport between other tissues. The nature of the matrix decides each tissue's role.

items.exam_note: Examples of connective tissue and their cell types (osteocyte, chondrocyte, adipocyte) are often asked.

items.content: Different white blood corpuscles: Neutrophil (polymorphonuclear leucocyte), Eosinophil, Basophil; labels Cytoplasm and Nucleus point to parts of a WBC

teacher_understanding.question: What are neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are granular white blood cells (granulocytes) with lobed nuclei. The neutrophil is called polymorphonuclear because its nucleus has many lobes.

teacher_understanding.question: How does each help the body?
teacher_understanding.answer: Neutrophils engulf bacteria (phagocytosis). Eosinophils fight parasites and are involved in allergy. Basophils release histamine during inflammation.

items.exam_note: The most abundant WBC (neutrophil) is a common question.

items.content: Lymphocyte, Monocyte, Platelets

teacher_understanding.question: What are lymphocytes and monocytes?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are agranular WBCs. Lymphocytes (B and T cells) give specific immunity, including antibody production. Monocytes become macrophages that engulf microbes.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are platelets important?
teacher_understanding.answer: Platelets are cell fragments that help blood clot at a wound and stop bleeding.

items.exam_note: Platelets and clotting; lymphocytes and antibodies.

items.content: Red blood corpuscle, pointing to a round biconcave cell without a nucleus

teacher_understanding.question: What does the RBC do?
teacher_understanding.answer: It carries oxygen using haemoglobin.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does a mammalian RBC lack a nucleus?
teacher_understanding.answer: Losing the nucleus leaves more space for haemoglobin, and the biconcave shape increases surface area for gas exchange.

items.exam_note: An enucleated RBC is a frequent fact.

items.content: Haversian canal (contains blood vessels and nerve fibres), pointing to the central canal of the concentric rings of bone

teacher_understanding.question: What is the Haversian canal?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a central channel in compact bone that carries blood vessels and nerve fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does bone need such canals?
teacher_understanding.answer: Bone is hard and living. Its cells need nutrients and oxygen, and the canals bring blood deep into the hard matrix.

items.exam_note: The Haversian system is characteristic of mammalian compact bone.

items.content: Canaliculus (contains slender process of bone cell or osteocyte)

teacher_understanding.question: What is a canaliculus?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a tiny channel in bone that holds the thin extensions of osteocytes (bone cells).

teacher_understanding.question: How do canaliculi keep bone cells alive?
teacher_understanding.answer: They connect the osteocytes to one another and to the Haversian canal, so nutrients and wastes can pass through the hard matrix.

items.exam_note: Remember: osteocyte = bone cell.

items.content: Chondrocyte and Hyaline matrix, pointing to cartilage cells and the clear surrounding matrix

teacher_understanding.question: What is hyaline cartilage made of?
teacher_understanding.answer: It consists of chondrocytes (cartilage cells) in a clear, firm matrix of proteins and sugars.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is it found?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is found at the ends of bones in joints, in the nose, the ear (as cartilage), the trachea and the larynx.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is cartilage used there instead of bone?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its matrix is firm yet flexible, so it smooths joint surfaces and gives shape that can bend.

items.exam_note: Chondrocyte = cartilage cell.

items.content: Reticular fibre, Fibroblast, Macrophage, Collagen fibre, Mast cell, Plasma cell

teacher_understanding.question: What cells and fibres make up areolar tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Fibroblasts produce the fibres (collagen and reticular). Macrophages engulf microbes. Mast cells release histamine. Plasma cells make antibodies.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is areolar tissue found?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lies between skin and muscles, around blood vessels and nerves, and in bone marrow. It fills spaces inside organs.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does it contain immune cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lies just under the skin and around organs, where microbes may enter, so it also helps repair tissues and defend the body.

items.exam_note: Areolar tissue is the 'packing' tissue between skin and muscle.

items.content: Fat droplet, Nucleus, Adipocyte, pointing to large fat-filled cells with the nucleus pushed to one side

teacher_understanding.question: What is adipose tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is connective tissue made of adipocytes, which are cells filled with fat droplets.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does it matter to the body?
teacher_understanding.answer: It stores energy as fat and acts as a thermal insulator, for example under the skin. It also cushions organs.

items.exam_note: Adipose tissue gives insulation, for example blubber in whales.

items.content: Fig. 6.10: Types of connective tissues: (a) types of blood cells, (b) compact bone, (c) hyaline cartilage, (d) areolar tissue, (e) adipose tissue

teacher_understanding.question: Which connective tissues does the caption list?
teacher_understanding.answer: Blood, compact bone, hyaline cartilage, areolar tissue and adipose tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How do they differ in matrix?
teacher_understanding.answer: The matrix is fluid in blood, hard in bone, firm and flexible in cartilage, loose and fibrous in areolar tissue, and mostly fat-filled cells in adipose tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is blood a connective tissue though it is fluid?
teacher_understanding.answer: It has cells in an intercellular matrix (plasma), and it connects body parts by transporting gases, nutrients and hormones.

items.exam_note: 'Blood is a connective tissue' is an exam staple.

items.content: Title: 'How do neurons transmit impulses (send message to other cells)?' Two orange neurons are shown. At the lower left, the axon of a previous neuron meets the first neuron's dendrites at a synapse (circled). The first neuron's cell body and nucleus give rise to a long axon. A blue arrow labelled 'electrical signal' runs along the axon towards its branched axon tips. The tips form a synapse (circled) with the dendrites of the next neuron, whose cell body and nucleus are labelled. The sequence is dendrites → cell body → axon → axon tips → synapse → next neuron's dendrites.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the diagram show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows the path of a nerve impulse through one neuron and across a synapse to the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the impulse travel?
teacher_understanding.answer: Dendrites receive a signal and pass it to the cell body. From there it travels along the axon as an electrical signal to the axon tips. At the synapse it is passed to the dendrites of the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the signal cross the synapse?
teacher_understanding.answer: A synapse is a tiny gap. The electrical signal reaching the axon tips causes release of chemicals (neurotransmitters), which cross the gap and start a new electrical signal in the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the impulse move in one direction only?
teacher_understanding.answer: Neurotransmitters are released only from axon tips and received only by the next neuron's dendrites, so the message flows one way.

items.exam_note: The direction of impulse flow and the parts of a neuron (dendrite, axon, synapse) are frequently asked.

items.content: axon of previous neuron, pointing to the incoming fibre at the left that ends at the first synapse

teacher_understanding.question: What is the 'axon of previous neuron'?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the axon of the neuron that sends the message into the first neuron shown.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is it shown?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows that neurons form chains, with one neuron's output becoming the next neuron's input.

items.exam_note: Shows that neurons connect in chains.

items.where_on_page: neuron diagram, circled at lower left and upper middle
items.content: synapse, pointing to the circled junctions between the axon ends and the dendrites of the next neuron

teacher_understanding.question: What is a synapse?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the junction between the axon tip of one neuron and the dendrite of the next neuron.

teacher_understanding.question: How is a message passed there?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is passed chemically, through neurotransmitters released into the gap.

items.exam_note: The definition of a synapse is commonly asked.

items.content: neuron cell body, pointing to the central star-shaped part of each neuron

teacher_understanding.question: What is the cell body?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the main part of the neuron (cyton). It contains the nucleus and cytoplasm.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is it essential?
teacher_understanding.answer: It keeps the neuron alive by making proteins, and it combines the incoming signals before passing them to the axon.

items.exam_note: Part of a neuron.

items.where_on_page: neuron diagram, inside each cell body
items.content: nucleus, pointing to the dark dot in each neuron cell body

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the neuron's nucleus?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is in the cell body.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does this matter?
teacher_understanding.answer: The nucleus controls the cell. Mature neurons generally do not divide, so damage is hard to repair.

items.exam_note: The nucleus lies in the cyton.

items.where_on_page: neuron diagram, bottom of first neuron
items.content: dendrites, pointing to the short branched projections around the first neuron's cell body

teacher_understanding.question: What are dendrites?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are short, branched extensions of the cell body that receive signals.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are they highly branched?
teacher_understanding.answer: Branching gives more surface area to receive signals from many neurons.

items.exam_note: Dendrites receive; the axon carries the signal away.

items.content: axon, pointing to the long single fibre from the first neuron's cell body towards the next neuron

teacher_understanding.question: What is the axon?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a long single fibre that carries the impulse away from the cell body.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the signal travel fast along it?
teacher_understanding.answer: Many axons are wrapped in a myelin sheath, which speeds up conduction of the impulse.

items.exam_note: The axon is the longest part of a neuron.

items.where_on_page: neuron diagram, blue arrow along the axon
items.content: electrical signal, a blue arrow running along the axon from the cell body towards the axon tips

teacher_understanding.question: What is the electrical signal?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the nerve impulse moving along the axon.

teacher_understanding.question: How is it generated?
teacher_understanding.answer: Ions such as sodium and potassium move across the neuron membrane, and this creates a travelling change in voltage.

items.exam_note: Impulses are electrical along the axon and chemical at the synapse.

items.content: axon tips, pointing to the branched endings of the axon near the next neuron

teacher_understanding.question: What are axon tips?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are the terminal branches of the axon that form synapses.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are they important?
teacher_understanding.answer: They release neurotransmitters to pass the message on to the next neuron.

items.exam_note: Also called axon terminals.

items.content: dendrites of next neuron, pointing to the branches of the second neuron that receive the signal

teacher_understanding.question: What do the dendrites of the next neuron do?
teacher_understanding.answer: They receive the message across the synapse.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this continue the message?
teacher_understanding.answer: They start a new impulse in the second neuron, which then repeats the same path.

notes.about: This page integrates a muscle-type comparison with diagrams of connective tissues and neuron-to-neuron signalling. The submission covers most content and provides substantial explanations, but contains incorrect outside information, some incorrect basis labels, and incomplete capture of diagram morphology.
key_questions: Can students distinguish the three muscle types by structure, location, function and control?
Can students identify the connective-tissue structures and relate their features to their functions?
Can students trace an impulse through a neuron and across a synapse?

decisions.decision: Accept simplified textbook descriptions such as cardiac muscle having one central nucleus.
decisions.reason: These match the source and are appropriate at this examination level.

decisions.decision: Require outside additions within otherwise source-based answers to be identified as outside knowledge.
decisions.reason: Correct additional information is still not information supplied by this page.

The source's term 'eccentric' for skeletal-muscle nuclei is compatible with the standard description 'peripheral'; it need not be treated as a factual discrepancy.

missing.what: The smooth-muscle illustration's spindle shape, with tapering ends, is not captured. The row records striations and the nucleus, but neither its content nor its answers identifies this visible, diagnostic cell shape.
missing.where_on_page: Muscle comparison table, bottom row, leftmost cell beneath 'Visceral (smooth muscle)'

missing.what: The areolar-tissue labels are listed without recording what their pointers identify. Capture the correspondence between reticular and collagen fibres and the illustrated fibre networks/bundles, and between each named cell and its depicted structure.
missing.where_on_page: Lower-left composite figure, panel (d), areolar tissue

wrong.problem: The answer to 'Where is it found?' includes the ear as a location of hyaline cartilage. The external ear is a standard example of elastic cartilage, not hyaline cartilage. The parenthetical 'as cartilage' does not resolve the incorrect answer to a hyaline-specific question.
wrong.fix: Remove the external ear from the hyaline-cartilage examples. Retain articular surfaces, nose, trachea and appropriate laryngeal cartilages; if mentioning the pinna, explicitly contrast its elastic cartilage.

wrong.problem: The matrix-comparison answer describes the adipose matrix as 'mostly fat-filled cells'. Cells are not extracellular matrix; the wording confuses the two components whose distinction the question is teaching.
wrong.fix: State that adipose tissue consists predominantly of closely packed fat-storing adipocytes with relatively little extracellular matrix. Keep the matrix distinct from the cells in this answer and in the related explanation in i6.

wrong.problem: Two answers marked 'book' contain information not provided on this page: attachment through tendons and movement at joints in the location answer, and somatic nervous-system control in the control answer.
wrong.fix: Split the source-supported facts from the explanations: mark 'location: skeleton' and 'voluntary' as book-based, and mark the tendon/joint and somatic nervous-system explanations as outside knowledge.

wrong.problem: The location–function explanation is labelled entirely 'book', although vessel narrowing/widening, the iris, attachment of muscles to hairs and goosebumps are explanatory additions not stated on the page.
wrong.fix: Retain the table's listed locations and functions as book-based, and separately mark the anatomical and mechanistic explanations as outside knowledge.

wrong.problem: The red blood corpuscle is assigned to panel (b). It belongs to the blood-cell panel (a), although its drawing is positioned below the compact-bone drawing in this composite.
wrong.fix: Change the location to 'Fig. 6.10 panel (a), red blood corpuscle drawn below the compact-bone illustration'.

checklist.note: Some outside additions are labelled book-based, and the hyaline-cartilage location answer contains an incorrect outside fact.
The explanations are generally substantial, but factual corrections and completion of diagram capture are needed before teacher acceptance.
The maker supplies the unit's scope, key questions, decisions with reasons and uncertainties, although the decisions focus on the patch rather than the full page.
No answer is visibly truncated or left as 'etc.'; grouped labels are explicitly named.
Most visible content is captured, but the smooth-muscle cell shape and areolar-label pointer correspondences are incomplete.
Only the running header and page number are treated as boilerplate; the substantive image content is recognised.
Each muscle-table row has its own item containing all four named column values.
Neuron labels and signal direction are well captured, but the areolar labels lack pointer-target descriptions and smooth-muscle morphology is omitted.
No equations or mathematical symbols requiring interpretation appear on this page.

The supplied questions generally go beyond restatement, explaining mechanisms, comparisons and functional significance. The principal deficiencies are accuracy and visual capture rather than general answer depth.
Basis labels need correction in i3 and i5; i12's outside answer misidentifies a cartilage example.
The heading, comparison rows, structural labels, caption and signalling process have sensible kinds and content types.
Prerequisites generally identify concrete concepts such as nuclei, matrix, muscle contraction and neuron parts.
Exam priorities are broadly sensible, and each question addresses its containing item. Empty cross-item test links do not create an evident mismatch.
The native text contains only the header and page number; no substantive text–image disagreement is evident.
